text:
Data centers ALREADY use a closed-loop heat exchange for their primary cooling loop, but then you need to reject that heat so it goes to a secondary heat exchange that typically uses fresh water in evap towers. THAT'S where you lose most of your water.
The new AI data centers are two orders of magnitude more power-hungry than "normal" data centers. For example, in Vegas there is a "large" Google data center that uses up 50MWh of power. The current largest proposed AI data center is 11,000MW or 220x the power demand of a previous generation data center.
The general rule is that you lose 1.8 gallons of fresh water to evaporation for every ton/hour of cooling. Every 1MW of power you pour into a data center needs 2.5 tons of cooling. For that 11GWh AI DC you would need 27,500 tons of cooling each hour. That's 49,500 gallons evaporated every hour, 1,188,000 lost every day.

You can't use salt water in those evap towers. -- Well you CAN, but they'll stop working by the end of day 1 because everything will be encased in minerals.
And here's the kicker... that's a VERY small part of the water that a DC will consume once you factor in how much water is required to generate the power in the first place.
The most prevalent power source for data centers (assuming they can get them as there is a massive multi-year backlog) is a combined-cycle natural gas turbine. They will use about 2,800 gallons of water per MWh generated. To generate enough power for that 11GWh data center, it would need 30,800,000 gallons of water each hour, 739,200,000 per day.
If the DC owners are willing to pay more and get a little less efficiency, they can reduce that to 200 gallons/MWh. That would still be 2,200,000 gallons an hour, 52,800,000 gallons a day -- And you'd have an even worse time with mineral build-up in the evap towers.

text:
The short answer is that is possible sometimes, but has other huge tradeoffs.

Reddit always gets this hilariously wrong, so it’s a lot of untangle from the common misconceptions.
First, the server side cooling loop is almost always closed loop. This is the side of the cooling system that collects all of the server heat. It’s also of never going to touch air or outside water because that would be a maintenance nightmare.
The open loop side that consumes water is an evaporation cooling tower. The server side cooling loop exchanges heat with the tower and outside environment through a heat exchanger. Essentially a shitload of water is sprayed on big coils that contain the heated server side water. The outside water evaporates using heat from that cooling water. Water has a large latent heat of evaporation, so a single cooling tower can be used to cool a large amount of servers, but it consumes water constantly.
The alternative is to use used forced convection in place of an open loop cooling tower. But the total air flow is absolutely gigantic. For a 10Mw data center we’re talking about around 1M CFM of air flow. That’s about an Olympic swimming pool sized air volume flowing every 5 seconds. It would require hundreds of large, loud fans. Data centers are already loud, so this would make the noise pollution much louder.
So, it can be done. Typically it requires more total energy but consumes no water. It’s certainly more expensive, to build, maintain and fuel, which is why corporations that don’t give a shit about the environment or the community around default to cooling towers.

The good news here is that 100% of the consumed water does return to earth, but the bad news is that it may not return to the same watershed.
